How this code-along works

The one question we keep asking: Can we find hidden groups in data without being told the answer, and does it help us?

So far every model in this course had an answer column to learn from: a price, a diagnosis, a yes or no. That is supervised learning. Here the answer column is gone. Unsupervised learning looks only at the measurements and tries to find structure in them: groups of similar rows (clustering) or a few directions that summarise many columns (PCA, Principal Component Analysis).

Each section follows the same six steps. Pick an answer under Predict first before you press ▶ Run; the real output and its explanation appear after the run.

Notebooks: week5-codealong-student.ipynb (fill in the TODOs) · week5-codealong.ipynb (complete code) · data in data/. Every output on this page comes from running the notebook top to bottom with Python 3.13, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6 and NumPy; in Colab, cluster numbers may be permuted and PCA signs flipped.

Short forms used on this page
Short form Stands for Plain meaning
PCA Principal Component Analysis finds the directions in which the data spreads most
PC1, PC2 first and second principal component the best and second-best of those directions
WCSS within-cluster sum of squares another name for k-means inertia
ARI Adjusted Rand Index how well two groupings agree: 1 = identical, 0 = chance
DBSCAN Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise groups are crowded regions; lonely points are noise
SVD Singular Value Decomposition the matrix routine scikit-learn uses to compute PCA
CDC / BRFSS Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System the US agency and its yearly health survey
BMI body mass index weight relative to height
SVM support vector machine the Week 4 champion classifier
ROC-AUC area under the ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve how well a model ranks positives above negatives: 0.5 = guessing, 1 = perfect
sd standard deviation the typical distance of a value from its column's average

Part 1 · Mall Customers: groups you can see ⏱ 40 min

A shopping mall recorded two numbers for 200 members of its loyalty card: annual income and a spending score from 1 to 100 that the mall assigns from purchase behaviour. Nobody labelled the customers with a type. Because there are only two columns, we can draw every customer as a dot and check the computer's answer against our own eyes.

1.1 Look at the data before modelling it

⏱ 5 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

A dataset with no answer column. Each row is one customer; the only question we can ask is whether some customers resemble each other more than others.

Why it matters

A mall cannot send 200 personal offers, but it can design a handful of campaigns. If customers fall into a few natural groups, each group gets its own campaign.

1.2 From scratch: k-means is assign → update → repeat

⏱ 15 min🛠 from scratch
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

k-means needs one number from you, k, the number of groups. Then it loops:

  1. Start: pick k customers at random and call them the centres.
  2. Assign: every customer joins the nearest centre (straight-line distance).
  3. Update: every centre moves to the average position of the customers who joined it.
  4. Repeat 2 and 3 until the centres stop moving.

Inertia (also called WCSS, within-cluster sum of squares) adds up each customer's squared distance to their own centre. Smaller inertia means tighter groups.

Why it matters

These four steps are the whole algorithm. Once you have written them yourself, KMeans in scikit-learn stops being a black box, and its settings (n_clusters, n_init, random_state) make sense.

🤔 Predict first

With k = 5 on these 200 customers, how many rounds of assign → update until the centres stop moving?

5 rounds with seed 0. Inertia can only go down or stay equal each round, so k-means always stops, usually within a handful of rounds.

Code it
def kmeans_scratch(X, k, seed=0, max_rounds=50, verbose=True):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    centres = X[rng.choice(len(X), size=k, replace=False)]   # START: k random customers become the centres
    history = [centres.copy()]
    for r in range(1, max_rounds + 1):
        dist = np.sqrt(((X[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2))   # distance of every point to every centre: shape (200, k)
        labels = dist.argmin(axis=1)   # ASSIGN: index of the nearest centre for every point
        inertia = ((X - centres[labels]) ** 2).sum()   # squared distance of every point to its own centre, added up
        new_centres = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])   # UPDATE: each centre moves to the mean of its points
        if verbose:
            print(f"round {r}: inertia {inertia:9.1f}")
        if np.allclose(new_centres, centres):   # REPEAT until the centres stop moving
            break
        centres = new_centres
        history.append(centres.copy())
    return centres, labels, inertia, history

C_scratch, lab_scratch, inertia_scratch, history = kmeans_scratch(X, k=5, seed=0)
print("final inertia", round(inertia_scratch, 1))

C_scratch, lab_scratch, inertia_scratch, history = kmeans_scratch(X, k=5, seed=0)
print("final inertia", round(inertia_scratch, 1))

# Watch the centres (black X) move: start, the first two updates, and the final position
steps = [0, 1, 2, len(history) - 1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.6), sharey=True)
for ax, i in zip(axes, steps):
    C = history[i]
    lab = np.sqrt(((X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)).argmin(axis=1)

    ax.set(title="start: random centres" if i == 0 else f"after update {i}" + (" (final)" if i == steps[-1] else ""), xlabel="income (k$)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("spending score")

What it means

k-means is nothing more than "join the nearest centre, move the centre to the middle, repeat", and on data with visible groups those three lines find them.

1.3 Swap in scikit-learn and confirm the same answer

⏱ 7 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

KMeans(n_clusters=5, n_init=10, random_state=42) runs the same loop, but with a smarter start (k-means++, which spreads the first centres apart) and 10 restarts, keeping the one with the lowest inertia. The ARI (Adjusted Rand Index) checks whether two labelings group the same points together: 1.0 means identical, even if the group numbers differ.

Why it matters

In real work you use the library, but you should be able to prove it does what you think. The second half of the cell shows why the restarts exist.

🤔 Predict first

Will scikit-learn find exactly the same five groups as your from-scratch loop?

Identical: same inertia 44,448.5, same centres, ARI 1.0. But two of the five random starts get stuck in a worse answer.

What it means

The library is our loop plus insurance: n_init=10 restarts protect against an unlucky start, which is why you should never set n_init=1 on real data.

1.4 Choosing k: the elbow and the silhouette

⏱ 7 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

We picked k = 5 by eye. Without a picture we need numbers.

  • Elbow method: inertia always drops as k grows (more centres, shorter distances), so look for the k where the drop suddenly gets small: the elbow of the curve.
  • Silhouette score: for each point compare a, its average distance to its own group, with b, its average distance to the nearest other group: s = (b − a) / max(a, b). Close to 1 means clearly in the right group, around 0 means on a border, negative means probably in the wrong group. The score is the average over all points.
Why it matters

Every clustering project has to justify its k, and the midterm practical asks for exactly that, with two numbers quoted.

🤔 Predict first

Which k will get the highest silhouette score?

k = 5, with silhouette 0.554, and the elbow is at 5 too.

Code it
ks = list(range(1, 11))
inertias, sils = [], []
for k in ks:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X)
    inertias.append(model.inertia_)   # store this k's inertia
    sils.append(silhouette_score(X, model.labels_) if k > 1 else np.nan)   # silhouette needs at least 2 clusters
    print(f"k={k:2d}  inertia {inertias[-1]:9.0f}  silhouette " + ("  -" if k == 1 else f"{sils[-1]:.3f}"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].plot(ks, inertias, "o-", color=COLORS[2]); ax[0].plot(5, inertias[4], "o", ms=14, mfc="none", mec=COLORS[1], mew=2.5)
ax[0].set(title="Elbow: inertia vs k", xlabel="k", ylabel="inertia (WCSS)")
ax[1].plot(ks[1:], sils[1:], "o-", color=COLORS[0]); ax[1].plot(5, sils[4], "o", ms=14, mfc="none", mec=COLORS[1], mew=2.5)
ax[1].set(title="Silhouette vs k (higher is better)", xlabel="k", ylabel="mean silhouette")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

What it means

Both numbers agree with our eyes: five groups. When the elbow and the silhouette agree you can choose k with confidence; when they disagree, the silhouette and what the groups mean in practice break the tie.

1.5 Read the five segments like a marketer

⏱ 6 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

A cluster is only useful once a person can describe it. We average each group's columns in the original units (dollars, score points, years) and give it a plain name.

Why it matters

Two customers can spend the same amount for very different reasons. A high earner who spends little needs a different message from a lower earner who spends a lot.

🤔 Predict first

Which segment do you expect to be the youngest on average?

Low income, high spending: average age 25.3. Age was never given to k-means, yet the groups differ in it.

Code it
mall["segment"] = km5.labels_   # attach each customer's group number
def describe(income, spend):
    i = "low" if income < 40 else "high" if income > 70 else "middle"
    s = "low" if spend < 40 else "high" if spend > 60 else "middle"
    return f"{i} income, {s} spending"

profile = mall.groupby("segment")[["Annual Income (k$)", "Spending Score (1-100)", "Age"]].mean().round(1)   # average of each column, per segment
profile["customers"] = mall["segment"].value_counts().sort_index()
profile["description"] = [describe(inc, sp) for inc, sp in profile.iloc[:, :2].to_numpy()]
print(profile.sort_values("Annual Income (k$)").to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
for j in range(5):
    m = km5.labels_ == j
    ax.scatter(X[m, 0], X[m, 1], s=26, color=COLORS[j], alpha=0.8)

ax.set(title="Five customer segments found by k-means", xlabel="Annual income (k$)", ylabel="Spending score (1-100)")

Segment A campaign that fits
high income, low spending untapped: premium brands and personal service to win them over

Palmer penguins

Part 2 · Penguins: did it rediscover the species? ⏱ 30 min

Researchers at Palmer Station, Antarctica measured 344 penguins of three species: Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. This time the true answer exists, so we can do something impossible in Part 1: hide the species from k-means, let it cluster, then lift the cover and check.

2.1 Two measurements, no species

⏱ 4 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

We keep two columns, bill length and flipper length, and put the species column aside as an answer key that the algorithm never sees.

Why it matters

This is a rehearsal for the real situation: if clustering can recover groups that we know exist, we can trust it more on data where nobody knows the groups.

🤔 Predict first

In the grey scatter, how many groups of penguins can you make out?

Most people see two or three: one cloud of long flippers on the right, and on the left a cloud that splits into short and long bills.

What it means

The groups are partly visible and partly overlapping, which makes this a fair test for k-means.

2.2 Cluster blind, then reveal the species

⏱ 8 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

We run k-means with k = 3 on the two measurements after scaling them (each column rescaled to average 0 and sd 1; section 2.3 shows why). Then we compare the clusters with the hidden species using the ARI (Adjusted Rand Index). The ARI asks, for every pair of penguins: did the clusters and the species both put this pair together, or both keep it apart? It is 1.0 for perfect agreement, about 0 for random groups, and it ignores what the groups are called.

Why it matters

This is the moment that makes unsupervised learning worth learning: when the groups are real, the algorithm finds them on its own. In practice, with new customers, unknown cell types or unlabelled documents, nobody can hand you the answer key, so the clusters are your first draft of it.

🤔 Predict first

What ARI do you expect between k-means' three clusters and the true species?

0.887. Almost every penguin lands with its own species, without a single label.

Code it
P2s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(P2)   # both columns rescaled to mean 0, sd 1 (section 2.3 shows why)
km_p = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(P2s)   # k-means with k = 3 on the scaled measurements
print(pd.crosstab(species, km_p.labels_, rownames=["true species"], colnames=["cluster"]).to_string())
print("\nARI, clusters vs true species:", round(adjusted_rand_score(species, km_p.labels_), 3))   # compare the clusters with the hidden answer key

# Colour each cluster like the species most of its members belong to, so the two panels can be compared
names = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]
sp_col = dict(zip(names, [COLORS[1], COLORS[4], COLORS[0]]))
majority = pd.crosstab(km_p.labels_, species).idxmax(axis=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), sharey=True)
ax[0].scatter(P2[:, 0], P2[:, 1], c=[sp_col[majority[c]] for c in km_p.labels_], s=22, alpha=0.8)
ax[0].set(title="What k-means found (no labels used)", xlabel="Bill length (mm)", ylabel="Flipper length (mm)")
for s in names:
    m = (species == s).to_numpy()
    ax[1].scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], color=sp_col[s], s=22, alpha=0.8, label=s)
ax[1].set(title="The true species (revealed)", xlabel="Bill length (mm)"); ax[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

2.3 Does scaling matter? Try it without

⏱ 6 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

k-means measures straight-line distance, which simply adds up the differences in each column. A column measured in big numbers therefore outvotes the others. Scaling (StandardScaler) turns every column into z-scores: z = (value − column mean) / column sd, so every column has average 0 and sd 1 and gets an equal vote.

Why it matters

Body mass is recorded in grams (sd about 800) while bill length is in millimetres (sd about 5). Without scaling, a 1-gram difference counts as much as a 1-millimetre difference, so weight decides everything.

🤔 Predict first

We now cluster on all four measurements, including body mass in grams. Without scaling, will the ARI go up, stay about the same, or collapse?

Collapse: unscaled ARI 0.314 against 0.793 scaled. Even with only the two millimetre columns, scaling lifts the ARI from 0.644 to 0.887.

Code it

P4 = peng[cols4].to_numpy()
print("sd of each column:", peng[cols4].std().round(1).to_dict())

def ari_k3(data):
    labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit_predict(data)
    return adjusted_rand_score(species, labels)

P4s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(P4)   # scale all four columns
print(f"2 columns:  unscaled ARI {ari_k3(P2):.3f}   scaled ARI {ari_k3(P2s):.3f}")
print(f"4 columns:  unscaled ARI {ari_k3(P4):.3f}   scaled ARI {ari_k3(P4s):.3f}")   # unscaled vs scaled, four columns

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2), sharey=True)
for a, data, t in [(ax[0], P4, "4 columns, UNSCALED"), (ax[1], P4s, "4 columns, scaled")]:

The sds are 5.5, 2.0 and 14.1 for the three millimetre columns and 802.0 for body mass. Unscaled, the four-column clustering scores ARI 0.314, and the left plot shows why: the clusters are horizontal slices by weight. Scaled, it scores 0.793; on the right the two lower clusters overlap in this view because they differ in bill shape, which this plot does not show. On the two millimetre columns scaling still helps, from 0.644 to 0.887. Notice too that four scaled columns (0.793) do worse than two (0.887): extra columns that do not separate the species add noise.

What it means

Always scale before k-means (and before PCA); otherwise the column with the biggest units quietly makes the decision.

2.4 Hierarchical clustering and the dendrogram

⏱ 6 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering starts with every penguin as its own group, then repeatedly merges the two closest groups until one remains. The dendrogram is a tree of those merges: the height of each join shows how different the two merged groups were. Cutting the tree with a horizontal line gives the clusters; you choose k after seeing the tree.

Why it matters

You often do not know k in advance. A dendrogram shows the options at once: a long vertical gap before a merge means the groups below it are clearly distinct.

🤔 Predict first

Where will the dendrogram show its tallest gaps: suggesting 2, 3 or 6 groups?

The two tallest joins sit at the top, so cutting below them gives three groups, matching the species (ARI 0.890).

Code it
Z = linkage(P2s, method="ward")   # merge history; "ward" merges the pair that adds the least inertia
cut = (Z[-3, 2] + Z[-2, 2]) / 2   # a height between the 2nd and 3rd biggest merges -> 3 groups
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.8))
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode="lastp", p=30, color_threshold=cut, no_labels=True, ax=ax)
ax.axhline(cut, ls="--", color=COLORS[1]); ax.set(title="Dendrogram of 342 penguins (last 30 merges shown)", ylabel="merge distance")
plt.show()

agg = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage="ward").fit_predict(P2s)   # hierarchical clustering cut into 3 groups
print("hierarchical (ward, 3 groups) ARI vs species: %.3f" % adjusted_rand_score(species, agg))

Z = linkage(P2s, method="ward")   # merge history; "ward" merges the pair that adds the least inertia
cut = (Z[-3, 2] + Z[-2, 2]) / 2   # a height between the 2nd and 3rd biggest merges -> 3 groups
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.8))
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode="lastp", p=30, color_threshold=cut, no_labels=True, ax=ax)
ax.axhline(cut, ls="--", color=COLORS[1]); ax.set(title="Dendrogram of 342 penguins (last 30 merges shown)", ylabel="merge distance")
plt.show()

agg = ...  # TODO: hierarchical clustering cut into 3 groups: AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage="ward").fit_predict(P2s)
print("hierarchical (ward, 3 groups) ARI vs species: %.3f" % adjusted_rand_score(species, agg))
Read the output
hierarchical (ward, 3 groups) ARI vs species: 0.890

Below the dashed cut line the tree splits into three coloured branches; above it, the last two merges are much taller than any merge below. Cutting there gives three groups with ARI 0.890 against the species, almost the same as k-means' 0.887.

What it means

Hierarchical clustering reaches a similar answer by a different route and lets you see how many groups are reasonable before you commit to k.

2.5 DBSCAN, and which method to use when

⏱ 6 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) defines a cluster as a crowded region: points with at least min_samples neighbours within distance eps grow a cluster outward; isolated points get the label −1, noise. You do not choose k. The test data here are two interlocking half-moons, a shape where the right answer is obvious to a person.

Why it matters

k-means assumes round, similar-sized blobs because every point joins its nearest centre. Real shapes (roads, rivers, fraud rings) are often long and curved, and some points belong to no group.

🤔 Predict first

Which method will separate the two moons perfectly?

Both of the last two score ARI 1.000; k-means scores 0.234 because it cuts straight across both moons.

Code it
Xm, ym = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.06, random_state=0)   # ym = the true moon of each point, used only to score
models = {"k-means (k=2)": KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0),
          "hierarchical, single link": AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage="single"),
          "DBSCAN (eps=0.2)": DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6))
for a, (name, model) in zip(ax, models.items()):
    lab = model.fit_predict(Xm)   # fit the model and get one label per point
    score = adjusted_rand_score(ym, lab)
    a.scatter(Xm[:, 0], Xm[:, 1], c=[COLORS[j] if j >= 0 else "#999999" for j in lab], s=14)
    a.set(title=f"{name}: ARI {score:.3f}", xticks=[], yticks=[])
    print(f"{name:26s} ARI {score:.3f}   noise points {(lab == -1).sum()}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Xm, ym = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.06, random_state=0)   # ym = the true moon of each point, used only to score
models = {"k-means (k=2)": KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0),
          "hierarchical, single link": AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage="single"),
          "DBSCAN (eps=0.2)": DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6))
for a, (name, model) in zip(ax, models.items()):
    lab = ...  # TODO: fit the model and get one label per point: model.fit_predict(Xm)
    score = adjusted_rand_score(ym, lab)
    a.scatter(Xm[:, 0], Xm[:, 1], c=[COLORS[j] if j >= 0 else "#999999" for j in lab], s=14)
    a.set(title=f"{name}: ARI {score:.3f}", xticks=[], yticks=[])
    print(f"{name:26s} ARI {score:.3f}   noise points {(lab == -1).sum()}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
Read the output
k-means (k=2)              ARI 0.234   noise points 0
hierarchical, single link  ARI 1.000   noise points 0
DBSCAN (eps=0.2)           ARI 1.000   noise points 0

k-means scores ARI 0.234: its boundary is a straight line that gives each moon's tip to the other cluster. Single-link hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN both score 1.000, with zero noise points.

Method You choose Shape of groups Good for Watch out for
k-means k round, similar size quick first segmentation of many rows must scale; sensitive to outliers
Hierarchical where to cut the tree depends on linkage (ward ≈ round, single = chains) small data where you want to see the options slow on very many rows (all pairwise distances)
DBSCAN eps, min_samples any shape, any number odd shapes, finding outliers (label −1) groups of very different density; eps must suit the scale
What it means

No method is best everywhere: pick the one whose idea of a "group" matches the shape of your data.

ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means

The inertia curve bends gently with no sharp elbow (123,389 at k = 2 down to 79,585 at k = 8). The silhouette is highest at k = 2 (0.267), drops to 0.163 at k = 3, recovers slightly to 0.174 at k = 4, and stays between 0.15 and 0.17 after that. On the same 0–0.6 axis as Mall, every value is low.

What it means

A low silhouette here is not a bug: health habits vary smoothly between people, so the groups overlap. We choose k = 4 because four groups give more useful, still readable profiles than two, and the silhouette at 4 is slightly better than at 3 or 5.

Why it matters

A public-health team cannot use "cluster 2". It can use "people with high blood pressure who are otherwise active", and it can see which profile has a far higher diabetes rate than average.

3.4 How we judge clusters: three metrics

⏱ 5 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept
Metric Needs true labels? What it measures Read it as
Inertia (WCSS) no total squared distance to own centre lower = tighter, but always falls as k grows; use the elbow
Silhouette no own-group closeness vs nearest-other-group closeness −1 to 1; higher = better separated
ARI yes agreement between clusters and a known grouping 1 = identical, 0 = chance

Inertia and the silhouette are internal checks: they work on any data. The ARI is an external check: it needs an answer key, so it is for testing a method (penguins) or comparing with a known grouping.

Why it matters

On the job you rarely have the answer key, so you combine internal scores with a sanity check: do the profiles make sense to someone who knows the domain?

🤔 Predict first

What ARI do you expect between the four health profiles and the two diabetes classes (yes / no)?

0.067, close to zero, and that is expected: four lifestyle profiles are a different grouping from two diagnosis classes.

penguins, then CDC

Part 4 · PCA: making a picture of high-dimensional data ⏱ 35 min

The CDC data had no picture because it has ten dimensions and a screen has two. PCA (Principal Component Analysis) finds the few directions along which the data spreads the most and redraws every row in those new coordinates. We build it by hand on the four penguin measurements, check it against scikit-learn, then use it to draw the CDC survey.

4.1 From scratch: centre → covariance → eigenvectors → project

⏱ 12 min🛠 from scratch
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

Four steps, each one line of NumPy:

  1. Centre: subtract each column's mean so the cloud of points sits around zero.
  2. Covariance: a 4 × 4 table of how every pair of columns moves together (positive = up together).
  3. Eigenvectors: the directions of that table's spread. Each comes with an eigenvalue, the amount of spread along it. The biggest one is PC1 (first principal component), the next is PC2, and so on, each at right angles to the ones before.
  4. Project: each penguin's new coordinates are its position measured along PC1 and PC2: two numbers instead of four.

Dividing each eigenvalue by their total gives the explained variance ratio: the share of all the spread that a component keeps.

Why it matters

When a picture needs two axes but the data has four (or ten, or a thousand) columns, PCA picks the two axes that lose the least information. The same idea compresses images and builds the 2-D maps of word and image embeddings used in modern AI.

🤔 Predict first

How many of the four penguin components do we need to keep 90% of the spread?

3. PC1 alone keeps 68.8%, PC1 + PC2 keep 88.2%, just short of 90%, and three keep 97.3%.

Code it
Z4 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(P4)   # scale the four measurements first, as in 2.3
centred = Z4 - Z4.mean(axis=0)   # step 1 CENTRE: subtract each column's mean
cov = centred.T @ centred / (len(centred) - 1)   # step 2 COVARIANCE: how each pair of columns moves together (4 x 4)
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)   # step 3 EIGENVECTORS (directions) and EIGENVALUES (spread along each)
order = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]   # sort from most spread to least
eigvals, eigvecs = eigvals[order], eigvecs[:, order]
scores = centred @ eigvecs[:, :2]   # step 4 PROJECT: coordinates along PC1 and PC2

print("covariance matrix:\n", pd.DataFrame(cov, index=cols4, columns=cols4).round(2).to_string())
print("\nspread along each direction (eigenvalues):", eigvals.round(3))
print("explained variance ratio:", (eigvals / eigvals.sum()).round(3))
print("cumulative:              ", np.cumsum(eigvals / eigvals.sum()).round(3))
print("PC1 direction (weights):", dict(zip(cols4, eigvecs[:, 0].round(2).tolist())))

The covariance table shows flipper length and body mass moving together strongly (0.87), while bill depth moves against both (−0.58 and −0.47). The eigenvalues are 2.762, 0.775, 0.366 and 0.109, so the explained variance ratios are 0.688, 0.193, 0.091 and 0.027, and the cumulative share reaches 0.882 with two components and 0.973 with three. PC1 gives bill length (−0.46), flipper length (−0.58) and body mass (−0.55) one sign and bill depth (0.40) the other: it is a "big penguin with a long, shallow bill" direction (the overall sign is arbitrary).

What it means

PCA is four lines of linear algebra: centre, measure how columns move together, find the main directions, and redraw the data along them.

4.2 Swap in scikit-learn and see the penguins in 2-D

⏱ 6 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

PCA() in scikit-learn gives the same components. Internally it uses the SVD (Singular Value Decomposition) of the centred data instead of the covariance table; mathematically the two routes give the same directions. A direction and its exact opposite describe the same line, so a component may come out with all its signs flipped.

Why it matters

Checking the library against your own code is how you learn to trust it, and the 2-D picture is the payoff: four measurements, one flat map.

🤔 Predict first

On the PC1–PC2 map, will the three species be separated?

All three mostly separated: Gentoo far to one side along PC1, Adelie and Chinstrap split along PC2.

Code it
pca_p = PCA().fit(Z4)   # scikit-learn PCA on the scaled penguin measurements
print("scikit-learn explained variance ratio:", pca_p.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
print("same directions as ours (ignoring sign)?", np.allclose(np.abs(pca_p.components_), np.abs(eigvecs.T)))
S2 = pca_p.transform(Z4)[:, :2]   # project onto the first two components
print("same 2-D coordinates (ignoring sign)?", np.allclose(np.abs(S2), np.abs(scores)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.8))
for s in names:
    m = (species == s).to_numpy()
    ax.scatter(S2[m, 0], S2[m, 1], color=sp_col[s], s=22, alpha=0.8, label=s)
r = pca_p.explained_variance_ratio_
ax.set(title="Four measurements drawn in 2-D with PCA", xlabel=f"PC1 ({r[0]:.1%} of spread)", ylabel=f"PC2 ({r[1]:.1%} of spread)"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

4.3 CDC: how many components for 90%? (scree plot)

⏱ 7 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

A scree plot shows each component's explained variance ratio as a bar, with the running total as a line. A common rule is to keep enough components to reach 90% of the spread.

Why it matters

Each component kept is one column for the next model. If 10 columns compress to 3 without losing much, models get faster and plots become possible; if they do not, PCA will not save you much.

🤔 Predict first

How many of the 10 CDC components are needed to keep 90% of the spread?

8. PC1 keeps only 26.0%: unlike the penguins, no single direction dominates.

print("components needed for 90%:", int(np.argmax(evr.cumsum() >= 0.90)) + 1)   # first number of components whose cumulative share reaches 0.90

CDC + Week 4 champion

Part 5 · Does it help a real model? ⏱ 5 min

The second half of the big question: we found groups, but do they make the Week 4 champion, a tuned SVM (support vector machine), better at predicting diabetes?

5.1 An honest negative result

⏱ 5 min
ConceptWhy it mattersPredictCode itRead the outputWhat it means
Concept

We score three versions of the Week 4 SVM with 5-fold cross-validation ROC-AUC (area under the ROC curve; 0.5 = guessing, 1 = perfect ranking): the original 21 features; the 21 features plus each person's cluster number (one-hot, k-means fitted inside each fold so nothing leaks); and the features compressed by PCA to 90% of the spread. This cell takes about 15–60 seconds.

Why it matters

Unsupervised steps are often sold as automatic improvements. The only way to know is to measure, with the same folds and no leakage.

🤔 Predict first

Which version scores the highest ROC-AUC?

The original features (0.8224). Adding clusters gives 0.8210 and PCA gives 0.8155, both slightly lower.

Code it
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline, make_union
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

class ClusterOneHot(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Fits k-means on the training fold only; outputs one 0/1 column per cluster."""
    def __init__(self, k=4): self.k = k
    def fit(self, X, y=None): self.km_ = KMeans(n_clusters=self.k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X); return self
    def transform(self, X): return np.eye(self.k)[self.km_.predict(X)]

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
idx = [list(X_train.columns).index(c) for c in health]   # the cluster step sees only the 10 health columns
champ = lambda: SVC(kernel="rbf", C=10, gamma=0.001, class_weight="balanced")   # Week 4 tuned SVM
variants = {
    "SVM, 21 features (Week 4)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), champ()),
    "SVM + cluster one-hot": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), make_union(FunctionTransformer(), ColumnTransformer([("c", ClusterOneHot(4), idx)])), champ()),
    "SVM on PCA (90% of spread)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=0.90), champ()),
}
for name, model in variants.items():
    s = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1)   # 5-fold cross-validated ROC-AUC
    print(f"{name:28s} ROC-AUC {s.mean():.4f} ± {s.std():.4f}")
Read the output
SVM, 21 features (Week 4)    ROC-AUC 0.8224 ± 0.0094
SVM + cluster one-hot        ROC-AUC 0.8210 ± 0.0094
SVM on PCA (90% of spread)   ROC-AUC 0.8155 ± 0.0073

The Week 4 SVM scores 0.8224, adding the cluster columns gives 0.8210 and PCA at 90% gives 0.8155. All three differences are smaller than the fold-to-fold variation (± about 0.01).

What it means

For this prediction task clustering and PCA do not help: the SVM already uses everything the clusters summarise. Their value here is understanding (profiles and a map), not accuracy, and reporting that honestly is part of the job.

Wrap-up

The answer to the big question

Can we find hidden groups without being told the answer? Yes, when the groups are real. k-means found the five mall segments our eyes saw (silhouette 0.554) and rediscovered three penguin species without a label (ARI 0.887). On the CDC survey the groups overlap (silhouette 0.174 at k = 4), but they still form four readable health profiles, and PCA gave us the picture that ten dimensions hid.

Does it help us? It helps us understand data: segments to market to, profiles to target, a map to explore. It did not make the Week 4 diabetes model more accurate (0.8224 without vs 0.8210 with clusters). Both answers come from measuring, not assuming.

Three habits to keep: scale first (ARI 0.314 → 0.793 on the penguins), justify k with two numbers (elbow and silhouette), and name your clusters in original units.

Self-check: 15 quick questions

⏱ 12 min
Score 0 / 0 answered

Q1 Week 1 A bank wants to predict how many dollars a customer will spend next month. What type of problem is this?

B. The target is a continuous number, so regression. Clustering would have no target at all.

Q2 Week 1 Which of these is an unsupervised task?

B. No answer column is given; the algorithm finds the topics itself.

Q3 Week 1 What is the correct order of the ML workflow?

B. Split first, so nothing about the test rows influences preparation or training.

Q4 Week 2 You fit a StandardScaler on the whole dataset and then split into train and test. What is wrong?

B. Fit every preprocessing step on the training rows only. This is a classic B6 bug.

Q5 Week 2 A column has 8% missing values and a few extreme outliers. Which simple fill is most robust?

B. One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median.

Q6 Week 2 Errors of a regression model are 2, −2 and 4. What is the RMSE (root mean squared error)?

B. Squares 4, 4, 16 → mean 8 → √8 = 2.83. 2.67 is the MAE (mean absolute error).

Q7 Week 3 A disease screen must miss as few sick people as possible. Which metric matters most?

B. Recall = share of the actual positives that the model catches.

Q8 Week 3 Why does KNN (k-nearest neighbours) need scaled features?

B. The same reason k-means needs scaling.

Q9 Week 3 What does 5-fold cross-validation give you that one train/validation split does not?

B. Five scores, so you see the mean and the ± spread.

Q10 Week 4 A decision tree scores 1.00 on training data and 0.71 on validation. What is happening?

B. Perfect on seen data, much worse on new data: limit depth or use a forest.

Q11 Week 4 In an RBF (radial basis function) SVM, what does a larger C do?

B. Large C = less tolerance for errors = a more complex boundary.

Q12 Week 5 k-means is run twice with k = 3 and the cluster numbers come out swapped (0↔2). What is the ARI between the two runs?

C. ARI only asks which points are together, not what the groups are called.

Q13 Week 5 Inertia keeps falling from k = 2 to k = 10. What should you conclude?

B. More centres always mean shorter distances.

Q14 Week 5 "PC1 explains 45% of the variance" means:

B. A component is a mixture of all features, not one of them.

Q15 Week 5 Your groups are curved and some points belong to no group. Which method fits best?

B. DBSCAN follows dense regions of any shape and labels lonely points −1 (noise). PCA is not a clustering method.

Mini practical: a 6-minute timed task

⏱ 15 min
6:00

Task (B5 style), 6 minutes, documentation only. The load_wine dataset has 178 wines with 13 chemical measurements. The grape variety (target) exists, but treat it as hidden until the last line.

  1. Scale the 13 columns.
  2. For k = 2 to 6, print inertia and silhouette, and choose k.
  3. Fit k-means with your k and draw a 2-D PCA plot coloured by cluster; print how much spread PC1 + PC2 keep.
  4. Only then compare your clusters with target using the ARI.

Then B6 style: the last two lines of the cell contain a bug. Find it, fix it and explain it in one sentence.

Self-mark (10 + 5): 4 for a k justified with two numbers, 3 for a labelled PCA plot, 3 for an interpretation that quotes numbers · B6: 2 find, 2 fix, 1 explain.

Starter (what students get)
wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
Xw, yw = wine.data, wine.target   # yw = grape variety: hidden until step 4
Ws = ...   # TODO 1: scale the 13 columns
# TODO 2: loop k = 2..6, print inertia and silhouette
# TODO 3: fit k-means with your k; PCA to 2 components; scatter coloured by cluster; print the share of spread kept
# TODO 4: ARI between yw and your cluster labels

# B6: this cell has a hidden bug. Find it, fix it, explain it.
bad = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xw)
print("ARI of the buggy clustering: %.3f" % adjusted_rand_score(yw, bad.labels_))
Model solution
wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
Xw, yw = wine.data, wine.target   # yw = grape variety: hidden until step 4
Ws = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xw)   # 1. scale
for k in range(2, 7):   # 2. choose k
    m = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Ws)
    print(f"k={k}  inertia {m.inertia_:7.1f}  silhouette {silhouette_score(Ws, m.labels_):.3f}")
kw = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Ws)   # 3. fit k = 3 and draw the PCA map
pw = PCA(n_components=2).fit(Ws); W2 = pw.transform(Ws)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.scatter(W2[:, 0], W2[:, 1], c=[COLORS[j] for j in kw.labels_], s=20)
ax.set(title="Wine: k-means (k=3) on a PCA map", xlabel="PC1", ylabel="PC2"); plt.show()
print("PC1 + PC2 keep %.3f of the spread" % pw.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())
print("ARI vs grape variety (revealed last): %.3f" % adjusted_rand_score(yw, kw.labels_))   # 4.

# B6 fixed. The bug: k-means was fitted on the UNSCALED Xw, so proline (sd ~315) outvotes hue (sd ~0.23).
bad = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xw)
print("buggy (unscaled) ARI %.3f   proline sd %.0f vs hue sd %.2f" % (adjusted_rand_score(yw, bad.labels_), Xw["proline"].std(), Xw["hue"].std()))
good = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Ws)   # fix: fit on the scaled Ws
print("fixed (scaled) ARI %.3f" % adjusted_rand_score(yw, good.labels_))

k=2  inertia  1658.8  silhouette 0.259
k=3  inertia  1277.9  silhouette 0.285
k=4  inertia  1175.4  silhouette 0.260
k=5  inertia  1109.5  silhouette 0.202
k=6  inertia  1046.0  silhouette 0.237
PC1 + PC2 keep 0.554 of the spread
ARI vs grape variety (revealed last): 0.897
buggy (unscaled) ARI 0.371   proline sd 315 vs hue sd 0.23
fixed (scaled) ARI 0.897

k = 3 has the highest silhouette (0.285, against 0.259 at k = 2 and 0.260 at k = 4), and the inertia curve bends there. PC1 + PC2 keep 0.554 of the spread and the three clusters separate along PC1. Revealed last, the clusters match the grape varieties with ARI 0.897. The bug: the unscaled fit scores only 0.371 because proline (sd 315) dominates every distance while hue (sd 0.23) has almost no say; fitting on Ws fixes it.
